What do you think of Big Pharma?

I'm not against vaccines and I encourage the geriatric patients I care for to get a flu vaccine every year along with the pneumococcal vaccine when they enter my facility. Pharmaceutical companies are a double edged sword. On one hand, the drugs that we give patients make a HUGE difference in their lives and really help them with many problems they have. EdIt: I don't know if something will come out of this but just recently a nurse from night shift made a huge medication error which could potentially injure three people. At our facility patients share insulin pens (to save money go figure.) The problem was this nurse gave the wrong pen that was used for three patients to one particular patient who had HIV and their own personal insulin pen. The nurse that morning recognized it was the same pen that was given to the HIV patient and realized it was given to the wrong patient and thus there is a small probability (2.5% and I say this with tongue in cheek) that the three patients who got that same pen may have been exposed to HIV. When you give an insulin pen there is a chance for blood to return to the pen. So this was a very preventable and stupid error/injury. This is why in school we are always told to triple check the treatments and meds we give always. This was a huge and preventable error. That nurse was fired and reported to the board. I have no idea if they told the patients because that's just a huge lawsuit waiting to happen.

What are hospital logistics like? Do things run smoothly or is it all FUBAR?

I've worked in long term care, rehabilitation and the hospital and I can tell you that in all three of these healthcare settings what makes an operation smooth or shit is management, staffing and state laws such as patient to aide/nurse ratio. You can work in one that runs smooth as pie and one that runs like complete shit. I've worked in shitty hospitals and shitty nursing homes. It really just depends on the facility.
What is usually the limiting factor? Is it a case of throwing money at the problem (e.g. hiring more aides) or removing red tape or what?

It's a combination of removing red tape and altering facility policy. Believe me if the ratio went down facilities would still give employees more patients illegally if they could save a dollar or two. The biggest problem is greed and quantity. As long as there is a body to cover a hall, management wont care. At one point in time I had over 20 patients to care for. I would challenge anyone to try to work a 12 hour shift under the same conditions that nurses and nursing assistants work and I can guarantee you they'll either quit or say its too much for little pay. We are overworked and underpaid. Not to mention if you're a good nursing assistant you do twice the work to cover the shit assistants. So add about 3 or more patients to that number. And if you don't have a nurse who backs you, its even worse. I've chewed many nurses out for coming to find me to put someone on a bedpan or change them when they could have spent the ten minutes themselves to do the task. It's not asking for much and nurses are trained to provide this type of care. 20-30 years ago nurses were doing ALL of the care. I couldn't imagine doing that in the conditions today.

Morphine is fucking awesome and a hell of a drug, especially when you give it to patients who are having chest pain. I've had morphine I.V. with a percocet once and I can tell you, I clearly was in a vegetative state.
